name: darkness & light

attributes.name: otherworld
attributes.value: source of power for this world

attributes.name: Manichaeism
attributes.attribute: treats light and dark as enemies

sources: Rees, Alwyn, and Brinely Rees. Celtic Heritage: Ancient Tradition in Ireland and Wales. London: Thames and Hudson, 1998.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Celts saw darkness and light as complementary. Modern people treat dawn as the start of day. The Celts began the day at evening. The day ended in the afternoon. The year began in fall. The year ended in summer. Celtic holidays fell on the night before the feast. Samhain fell on November 1. People celebrate it as Hallowe'en on October 31. No Celtic creation myth survives. The pattern suggests a shadowy world preceded our own. The otherworld is that separate connected place. Objects in this world gain power from it. Persian Manichaeism made light and dark enemies. The Celts did not treat them as antagonists. They were complementary parts of a single whole.
objective: This record documents the Celtic view that darkness and light were complementary parts of a single whole.
key_results: The Celtic day began at evening and ended in the afternoon.
The Celtic year began in fall and ended in summer.
Samhain on November 1 is celebrated as Hallowe'en on October 31.
Celtic darkness and light were complementary, unlike Manichaean opposites.
